meta.title: Mulch depth for Michigan beds: 2 to 3 inches | Grand Scapes
meta.description: MSU Extension says 2 to 3 inches of mulch is enough and more is not better. New beds, yearly top ups, trees, and what too much mulch does to your plants.

title: How deep mulch **should be.**
lede: Two to three inches is enough for most beds, and about an inch freshens a bed that already has mulch in it. That is MSU Extension's advice, and its plainest line is that more is not better. Here is how to measure what you have and what to add.
short: Most beds: 2 to 3 inches. MSU Extension says that is adequate, and more is not better.
Already mulched: a thin, 1 inch top dressing is more than adequate, MSU says.
A brand new bed can start at 3 to 4 inches, then about an inch a year.
Keep it thin at trunks and stems. MSU's rule is a 6 inch mulch free ring around trees.
Color is a matter of taste. In an MSU trial, most mulches worked equally well.

sections.h: Why the answer is two to three inches
p: MSU Extension has given the same answer for years: two to three inches of mulch is adequate, and more is not better. Its mulching FAQ says deeper is not always better, and that 2 to 3 inches gets the full benefit in most cases.

At that depth, mulch does its jobs. It slows evaporation so water reaches the roots, holds down weeds, adds organic matter as it breaks down and keeps the soil cooler. In one MSU trial, 3 inches of wood chips cut midday soil temperature by 18 degrees Fahrenheit.

table.note: MSU's tip sheet adds that wood mulch breaks down faster under automatic irrigation, and that dry spots keep more of their mulch each year and need smaller additions.

p: A bed that has been mulched every spring for a few years often has plenty already. Before adding any, pull the mulch back in three or four places and measure down to the soil with a tape. Check the back of the bed by the house as well as the front edge.

If you find 3 inches or more, skip the new layer this year or add just enough to cover the faded spots. If you find old mulch caked into a hard crust, MSU Extension says to break up the clods and pull the excess out toward the edge of the bed or the drip line. If you would rather not dig, ask Rob to check it when he comes out for an estimate.

list: **Smothered perennials.** MSU's Smart Gardening tip sheet says thick layers every season can smother plants, especially perennials, and that rots may be encouraged by too much organic material at the crown.

**A crust that sheds water.** As thick mulch dries, it can cake into a layer that resists rain and irrigation, MSU says, and it has to be broken up with a garden fork or hoe before water gets through.
**A barrier to water and nutrients.** MSU Extension warns that layers upon layers of dried mulch can become an impervious barrier.
**Roots in the wrong place.** Mulch piled at the base of a tree invites root rot and insects, and it increases surface rooting into the mulch itself, according to the same MSU article.

p: Never pile mulch against a trunk, the cone MSU calls a mulch volcano. One MSU rule is to keep a six inch ring around the base of the tree free of mulch. Another MSU article allows a thin, one inch layer right next to the trunk that gets thicker as it moves out. Either way, the trunk is bare or close to it, and the full depth is farther out.

MSU Extension also suggests grouping trees and shrubs into planted beds, where you can, instead of mulching a small circle around each one. One bed is also easier to edge and keep sharp than a lawn full of little rings.

The color is up to you. MSU's tip sheet says choosing a mulch is often based on personal preference and appearance, and color enhanced mulch is on its list. In an MSU trial that compared ground pine bark, hardwood bark, cypress and red ground pallet mulch, most of the mulches worked equally well.
We lay black, brown and red. Most of the finished beds in our photos are black mulch inside a gray block wall. If you are torn between colors, ask Rob when he comes out to look at the beds.

sections.h: Keeping the mulch in the bed
p: A border keeps the mulch at the right depth. A cut natural edge or a low block wall holds the mulch in the bed instead of letting it creep into the lawn, and it gives the mower a clean line to follow.

Our [mulch and flower bed makeovers](/mulch-and-flower-beds/) are weeded, edged, laid with fabric and finished with fresh mulch, and our [bed edging and block walls](/bed-edging-and-block-walls/) work covers the border itself.
